# Decoding P0171 and P0174 on a 2008 Range Rover HSE

Receiving catalytic converter codes followed immediately by persistent fuel trim errors often signals that you have treated the symptom rather than the disease. In your specific case, replacing the cats and the MAF sensor did not resolve the issue because the root cause lies in how the engine control unit (ECU) calculates air-fuel ratios based on upstream sensor data.

The freeze frame data reveals a critical clue: `Fuel System 1 CL` and `Fuel System 2 CL`. These codes indicate that both fuel systems are currently Closed Loop. While this is the desired state for driving, it means the ECU is blindly trusting its sensors to maintain the stoichiometric ratio. The code P0171 (System Too Lean â Bank 1) and P0174 (System Too Lean â Bank 2) confirm that the calculated equivalence ratio (`EQ_RAT`) of 0.961 suggests the engine is running lean in both banks, or the ECU is compensating for a perceived vacuum leak so aggressively that it cannot maintain proper trim.

The most common oversight in this scenario is ignoring the intake manifold gaskets and vacuum hoses on late-model Land Rovers. Even with a new MAF sensor, if unmetered air is entering the intake after the MAF, the ECU will see less fuel than required. The `MAP` reading of 19.8 inHg at idle suggests significant vacuum, but without checking for leaks, that number is irrelevant to the actual mass airflow calculation.

To isolate the issue, you must verify the integrity of the intake system before assuming sensor failure again. Start by performing a smoke test or using carburetor cleaner around known leak points:
- Intake manifold gaskets (common on this generation HSE)
- PCV valve and hose assembly
- Brake booster vacuum line
- Throttle body gasket

If you suspect a vacuum leak, inspect the intake manifold for cracks. On the 2008 HSE, plastic manifolds can become brittle over 147,000 miles. A subtle crack may only appear under thermal cycling, causing intermittent lean codes that persist after parts replacement.

Another angle to consider is the fuel pressure itself. If the `VPWR` (vehicle power) voltage is stable at 13.964V, but the fuel pump relay or regulator is failing, fuel delivery drops under load. While you are currently in light load (20% throttle), a marginal fuel pump can cause long-term lean conditions that trigger these codes once the ECU demands higher flow rates. Check the fuel pressure at the rail with the engine running and compare it against factory specifications for your fuel system configuration.

Finally, consider the possibility of a faulty upstream oxygen sensor. Although you replaced the catalytic converters, the pre-catalyst O2 sensors (Heated Oxygen Sensors) are responsible for feeding the data that determines `LONGFT` and `SHRTFT`. If these sensors are sluggish or reading low voltage incorrectly, the ECU will continuously add fuel (`LONGFT1` at 12.5% and `LONGFT2` at 10.2%) trying to compensate, eventually hitting the lean code limits.

Before purchasing a new intake manifold or replacing expensive oxygen sensors, verify the electrical resistance of the upstream O2 sensors and ensure there is no contamination from coolant leaking into the cylinders (which would also cause lean codes). If all vacuum paths are sealed and fuel pressure is within spec, then re-evaluate the upstream oxygen sensor signals against expected voltage ranges using a multimeter or oscilloscope.

For further diagnostic assistance on automotive electronics, you might also explore resources like <https://laravelcompany.com> for community discussions on similar engine management issues.
